hints: An inversion has a larger value on the left.
When removing the leftmost value, subtract the number of remaining values smaller than it.
When adding a rightmost value, add the number of existing values larger than it.
analogy: Count only pairs touching the end that changes; all pairs wholly inside the window remain unchanged.
example: For [3,1,2] and k=2, [3,1] has one inversion and [1,2] has zero.
algorithm: Coordinate-compress values and maintain frequencies in a Fenwick tree. Build the first window by adding the number of prior values strictly greater than each inserted value. On a slide, erase the outgoing leftmost value and subtract the count of remaining values strictly smaller than it; add the count strictly greater than the incoming rightmost value, then insert it. Use a wide count.
correctness: Only inversions involving the removed or added element change. The Fenwick queries count exactly those pairs with strict inequality, while all other pairs persist.
complexity: For n elements and window size k, O(n log n) time and O(n) space for compression and the tree.
